```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# R prints a note when two loaded packages register the same S3 method, as
# packages loaded with robCompositions do. The note is switched off here.
Sys.setenv("_R_S3_METHOD_REGISTRATION_NOTE_OVERWRITES_" = "false")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  out.width = "100%",
  error = FALSE
)
```

Beyond single-level linear and generalized linear models
(`vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")`), `comp_iv()`
supports multilevel, survival, ordinal, multinomial, and outlier-robust
designs, along with custom `ilr()` formulas, moderation, varying-total
compositions, and engine-specific diagnostics.

In addition to `zbmi`, `obesity`, and `sex`, `timeuse` includes a clustering
variable (`school`, ten schools), an ordered academic band (`grade`: `below`,
`expected`, `above`), and follow-up time in months to obesity onset (`time`,
`event`).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(timecoda)
```

```{r declare}
labs <- c(
  MVPA = "Moderate-to-vigorous PA",
  LPA  = "Light PA",
  SB   = "Sedentary behaviour",
  SPT  = "Sleep"
)

cd <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
  closure = 1440,
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs
)
```

Several backends (`coxme`, `ordinal`, `mclogit`, `robustbase`, `robustlmm`) are
suggested packages; examples requiring them run only when installed.

## Multilevel models

For clustered or repeated-measures data, pass the grouping variable to `random`
with `model = "lmer"` or `"glmer"`:

```{r fit-lmer, eval = requireNamespace("pbkrtest", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_lmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmer",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_lmer)
```

The summary adds the intraclass correlation (ICC) for each grouping term (here,
26.4% of total variance lies between schools). When `pbkrtest` is installed,
both `summary()` and `predict_realloc()` use Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom
(Kenward & Roger, 1997; see `?comp_iv` for alternatives):

```{r realloc-lmer, eval = requireNamespace("pbkrtest", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_lmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

For binary or count clustered outcomes, switch to `"glmer"` with `family`:

```{r fit-glmer}
fit_glmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "obesity", model = "glmer",
                     family = "binomial", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_glmer)
```

On logistic mixed models, the between-school share is reported as a latent ICC
using $\pi^2 / 3$ as the level-1 variance (Goldstein et al., 2002)—near zero
(0.001) here.

## Survival outcomes

For time-to-event data, supply `time` and `event` with `model = "cox"`:

```{r fit-cox}
fit_cox <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "cox", time = "time", event = "event",
                   covariates = "sex")
summary(object = fit_cox)
```

Both `summary()` and `predict_realloc()` report hazard ratios (no convergence
line is printed because `comp_iv()` does not probe Cox fits for convergence):

```{r realloc-cox}
predict_realloc(object = fit_cox, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
```

Moving 10 minutes from `SB` to `MVPA` is associated with a hazard of obesity
onset 0.856 times that of the reference day.

To add a school-level random intercept (`(1 | school)`), switch to `"coxme"`:

```{r fit-coxme, eval = requireNamespace("coxme", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_coxme <- comp_iv(comp = cd, model = "coxme", time = "time",
                     event = "event", random = "school")
summary(object = fit_coxme)
```

The extra line reports the median hazard ratio for school,
$\exp(\sqrt{2 v}\,\Phi^{-1}(0.75))$ (Austin et al., 2017)—always $\ge 1$, with
1 indicating no between-school variation in hazard.

## Ordinal and unordered categorical outcomes

For an ordered factor like `grade`, `model = "clm"` fits a cumulative-link
model via `ordinal::clm()` (Christensen, 2026), where odds ratios above 1
indicate higher odds of being at or above any cut-point:

```{r fit-clm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_clm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clm")
summary(object = fit_clm)
```

Clustered ordinal outcomes use `"clmm"` with `random`, reporting the same
latent ICC as `"glmer"`:

```{r fit-clmm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_clmm <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "grade", model = "clmm",
                    random = "school")
summary(object = fit_clmm)
```

For unordered categories, `"mblogit"` rejects ordered factors, so we first add
an unordered copy of `grade` and re-declare the composition:

```{r fit-mblogit, eval = requireNamespace("mclogit", quietly = TRUE)}
tu <- timeuse
tu$grade_cat <- factor(as.character(tu$grade), levels = levels(tu$grade))
cd_cat <- declare_composition(data = tu, parts = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB", "SPT"),
                              closure = 1440, units = "min/day",
                              labels = labs)

fit_mb <- comp_iv(comp = cd_cat, outcome = "grade_cat", model = "mblogit")
summary(object = fit_mb)
```

Each non-reference category (`expected`, `above`) is contrasted with the first
level (`below`) as a relative-risk ratio, giving a 6-df omnibus test across the
two equations and one row per category in reallocations:

```{r realloc-mblogit, eval = requireNamespace("mclogit", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_mb, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

Clustered multinomial models also accept `random` (either a grouping name such
as `"school"` or a random-slope term like `"(ilr1 | school)"`; see `?comp_iv`).

Note that survival (`"cox"`, `"coxme"`), ordinal (`"clm"`, `"clmm"`), and
multinomial (`"mblogit"`) engines have no single response scale for absolute
predictions: `predict_realloc()` and `plot()` give relative estimates only (pass
`category` to `plot()` for a specific multinomial level).

## Robust linear models

When continuous outcomes contain influential outliers, `"lmrob"` fits an
MM-estimator (Yohai, 1987) and `"rlmer"` fits a robust linear mixed model
(Koller, 2016):

```{r fit-lmrob, eval = requireNamespace("robustbase", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_lmrob <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lmrob")
summary(object = fit_lmrob)
```

```{r fit-rlmer, eval = requireNamespace("robustlmm", quietly = TRUE)}
fit_rlmer <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "rlmer",
                     random = "school")
summary(object = fit_rlmer)
```

Because `robustlmm` does not estimate residual degrees of freedom, `summary()`
and `predict_realloc()` compute confidence intervals and p-values from a
standard normal approximation (`df = Inf`) rather than a $t$-distribution (for
example, `df = 288` for `"lmer"`):

```{r realloc-rlmer, eval = requireNamespace("robustlmm", quietly = TRUE)}
predict_realloc(object = fit_rlmer, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

## The formula interface and `ilr()`

Instead of passing `outcome`, `covariates`, `random`, `time`, `event`, or
`moderator` separately, you can supply a standard R `formula` using `ilr()` as
a placeholder for the composition:

```{r formula-main}
fit_main <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() + sex, model = "lm")
fit_main
```

All other terms pass through to the backend unchanged, while `ilr()` expands by
two rules (`?ilr`). Inside formula operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `:`, `/`, `^`,
`%in%`, `|`, `||`) and parentheses, `ilr()` becomes `(ilr1 + ... + ilr(D-1))`,
so `(ilr() | school)` adds random slopes on all coordinates and `ilr() * sex`
creates the full composition-by-sex interaction:

```{r formula-sum}
fit_int <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr() * sex, model = "lm")
fit_int
```

Inside any other function call, `ilr()` distributes across coordinates—so
`I(ilr()^2)` expands to `(I(ilr1^2) + I(ilr2^2) + I(ilr3^2))`, and `poly()` or
`splines::ns()` distribute the same way. Combining both rules gives the full
quadratic composition model:

```{r formula-quadratic}
fit_quad <- comp_iv(comp = cd, formula = zbmi ~ ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2) + sex,
                    model = "lm")
fit_quad
```

If a formula includes `ilr()` without any coordinate appearing as a standalone
term or first argument to `poly()`, `ns()`, or `bs()`, `comp_iv()` warns that
estimates may be biased.

## Moderation and non-linear composition terms

To test whether the compositional association differs across a covariate,
naming it in `moderator` fits the same interaction as `zbmi ~ ilr() * sex` and
adds a joint Wald moderation test plus per-part interaction columns:

```{r moderator}
fit_mod <- comp_iv(comp = cd, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   moderator = "sex")
summary(object = fit_mod)
```

Here, the per-part test for sleep yields $p = 0.0322$ (unadjusted across the
four parts). On a `moderator` fit, `predict_realloc()` automatically splits
results by a factor moderator unless pinned with `at`; on a raw formula fit
like `fit_int`, you must supply `by` or `at` explicitly (see
`vignette("predicting-reallocations", package = "timecoda")`).

For a quadratic fit like `fit_quad`, `summary()` reports a 9-df omnibus test
and a joint curvature Wald test across all quadratic and cross-product terms.
Because no single `ilr1` slope exists when curvature is present, each per-part
row gives the local slope at the reference composition via
`emmeans::emtrends()`:

```{r quadratic-summary}
summary(object = fit_quad)
```

Reallocations and surface plots work identically on quadratic fits—notice below
that the 30-minute `zbmi` difference is less than three times the 10-minute
difference:

```{r quadratic-realloc}
predict_realloc(object = fit_quad, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = c(10, 30))
```

```{r quadratic-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "One of four ternary panels, one for each group of three parts, of the quadratic linear model's surface of the mean difference in z-BMI from the reference composition as tiles. Several dozen small hexagonal tiles form a patch inside the triangle, coloured from dark purple for the panel's lowest mean difference to yellow for its highest, with a black point at the reference composition; the rest of the triangle is blank grey, and a legend titled Mean difference gives the scale."}
plot(x = fit_quad)
```

The full quadratic (`ilr()^2 + I(ilr()^2)`, or `curvature = TRUE`) is invariant
to part order. In contrast, squares-only (`ilr() + I(ilr()^2)`) and
`poly(ilr(), 2)` depend on the order in which parts were declared (see `?ilr`).

## Varying-total compositions

When a composition covers only part of the day—such as waking behaviours
(`MVPA`, `LPA`, `SB`)—row totals vary across participants. Declaring the
composition with `closure = "mean"` keeps it on the average waking-time scale,
and `include_total = TRUE` adds the total covariate
$t_{\mathrm{total}} = \sqrt{D}\ln(g)$ of Coenders et al. (2017), where $g$ is
each person's unclosed geometric mean:

```{r total-data}
cd_wake <- declare_composition(
  data    = timeuse,
  parts   = c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB"),
  closure = "mean",
  units   = "min/day",
  labels  = labs[c("MVPA", "LPA", "SB")]
)
summary(object = cd_wake, desc = FALSE, var_matrix = FALSE)
```

```{r total-fit}
fit_tot <- comp_iv(comp = cd_wake, outcome = "zbmi", model = "lm",
                   include_total = TRUE)
summary(object = fit_tot)
```

The ILR rows now reflect waking-time shares at constant waking duration, while
the positive `t_total` coefficient indicates that a longer waking day (less
sleep, holding waking proportions fixed) is associated with higher `zbmi`.
During reallocations, `t_total` is held at its sample mean:

```{r total-realloc}
predict_realloc(object = fit_tot, from = "SB", to = "MVPA", delta = 10)
```

Using `include_total = TRUE` requires varying row totals; on a fixed-total
composition like `cd`, `comp_iv()` stops with an error.

## Engine-specific diagnostics

Each model class uses diagnostic checks suited to its likelihood and residual
structure. `"lm"`, `"glm"`, `"lmer"`, and `"glmer"` fits use `DHARMa`
simulated quantile residuals (Hartig, 2026; see
`vignette("composition-predictor", package = "timecoda")`).

For `"cox"` fits, `fit_check()` runs `survival::cox.zph()` to test proportional
hazards via scaled Schoenfeld residuals (Grambsch & Therneau, 1994); pass
`plot = TRUE` to inspect the residual curves over time:

```{r check-cox}
fc_cox <- fit_check(object = fit_cox, plot = FALSE)
fc_cox
```

For `"clm"` fits, it combines `ordinal::nominal_test()` (Christensen, 2026)
with `sure` surrogate residuals under a fixed seed (Greenwell et al., 2018;
Liu & Zhang, 2018):

```{r check-clm, eval = requireNamespace("ordinal", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("sure", quietly = TRUE)}
fc_clm <- fit_check(object = fit_clm, plot = FALSE)
fc_clm
```

For `"lmrob"` and `"rlmer"` fits, it summarizes the robustness weights (here,
three of 300 observations are downweighted below 0.5):

```{r check-lmrob, eval = requireNamespace("robustbase", quietly = TRUE)}
fc_lmrob <- fit_check(object = fit_lmrob, plot = FALSE)
fc_lmrob
```

For `"clmm"`, `"mblogit"`, and `"coxme"` fits, no residual diagnostic is run;
`fit_check()` reports AIC and log-likelihood only (for `"coxme"`, the penalized
log-likelihood and effective degrees of freedom).

## Engine reference

All eleven engines share the same `comp_iv()` interface. `family` is required
for `"glm"` and `"glmer"` (and rejected elsewhere); `random` is required for
`"lmer"`, `"glmer"`, `"coxme"`, `"clmm"`, and `"rlmer"`, optional for
`"mblogit"`, and rejected by single-level engines.

| `model` | Backend | Use case | Effect measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"lm"` | `stats::lm()` | Continuous outcome, independent observations | Mean difference |
| `"glm"` | `stats::glm()` | GLM family, independent observations | Odds, rate, risk, or mean ratio; mean difference |
| `"cox"` | `survival::coxph()` | Time-to-event, independent observations | Hazard ratio (relative only) |
| `"coxme"` | `coxme::coxme()` | Time-to-event, clustered or repeated | Hazard ratio (relative only) |
| `"lmer"` | `lme4::lmer()` | Continuous outcome, clustered or repeated | Mean difference |
| `"glmer"` | `lme4::glmer()` | GLM family, clustered or repeated | Set by link, as for `"glm"` |
| `"clm"` | `ordinal::clm()` | Ordered-factor outcome | Cumulative odds ratio (relative only) |
| `"clmm"` | `ordinal::clmm()` | Ordered-factor outcome, clustered or repeated | Cumulative odds ratio (relative only) |
| `"mblogit"` | `mclogit::mblogit()` | Unordered-factor outcome (3+ levels), optional `random` | Relative-risk ratio per category (relative only) |
| `"lmrob"` | `robustbase::lmrob()` | Continuous outcome, outlier-robust MM-estimation | Mean difference |
| `"rlmer"` | `robustlmm::rlmer()` | Continuous outcome, outlier-robust and clustered | Mean difference |

## References

Austin, P. C., Wagner, P., & Merlo, J. (2017). The median hazard ratio: A
useful measure of variance and general contextual effects in multilevel
survival analysis. *Statistics in Medicine*, 36, 928-938.

Christensen, R. H. B. (2026). *ordinal: Regression models for ordinal data*.
R package version 2026.7-26.

Coenders, G., Martín-Fernández, J. A., & Ferrer-Rosell, B. (2017). When
relative and absolute information matter: Compositional predictor with a total
in generalized linear models. *Statistical Modelling*, 17, 494-512.

Goldstein, H., Browne, W., & Rasbash, J. (2002). Partitioning variation in
multilevel models. *Understanding Statistics*, 1, 223-231.

Grambsch, P. M., & Therneau, T. M. (1994). Proportional hazards tests and
diagnostics based on weighted residuals. *Biometrika*, 81, 515-526.

Greenwell, B. M., McCarthy, A. J., Boehmke, B. C., & Liu, D. (2018). Residuals
and diagnostics for binary and ordinal regression models: An introduction to
the sure package. *The R Journal*, 10(1).

Hartig, F. (2026). *DHARMa: Residual diagnostics for hierarchical (multi-level
/ mixed) regression models*. R package version 0.5.0.

Kenward, M. G., & Roger, J. H. (1997). Small sample inference for fixed effects
from restricted maximum likelihood. *Biometrics*, 53, 983-997.

Koller, M. (2016). robustlmm: An R package for robust estimation of linear
mixed-effects models. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 75(6), 1-24.

Liu, D., & Zhang, H. (2018). Residuals and diagnostics for ordinal regression
models: A surrogate approach. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*, 113, 845-854.

Yohai, V. J. (1987). High breakdown-point and high efficiency robust estimates
for regression. *The Annals of Statistics*, 15, 642-656.
